paras: The shooting of Jack Hicks was the wounding of a Black man by a sheriff in South Carolina in late July or on 1 August 1881, as he ran from an attempted arrest. The sheriff fired four shots and hit Hicks twice, but Hicks escaped and was reported likely to die. The only account is a paragraph from the Williamsburg Herald, reprinted on 4 August in state-news columns in Anderson and Savannah.

According to the Williamsburg Herald, Hicks, described as "a colored man," had three indictments out against him. He was charged with stealing cotton, with "breaking jail and turning out prisoners," and with not paying his poll tax. The item does not name the place, and the county is suggested only by the name of the paper that first reported it.

The sheriff tried to arrest Hicks on a Monday morning, which the Herald called "last Monday morning." When the sheriff ordered him to surrender, Hicks ran, and the sheriff fired four shots at him. Two shots struck him, one in the shoulder "just above the blade" and one in the leg. Hicks "made good his escape," though the Herald added that "it is thought he will die."
No later report of Hicks's death, capture or trial, or of any inquiry into the shooting, appears in the coverage.

The Anderson Intelligencer and the Savannah Morning News both ran the Herald's paragraph on 4 August 1881 under the attribution "The Williamsburg Herald says," among other South Carolina items. Neither paper added a headline or comment, and the story was told entirely from the sheriff's side, closing on the list of charges against Hicks. In the Anderson paper it ran alongside other brief state notices, among them a fatal lamp explosion, a killing between brothers and a barn fire.

reader.title: Shooting of Jack Hicks
bases: A sheriff trying to arrest Jack Hicks on outstanding indictments fired four shots at him as he ran, wounding him twice; no crowd or mob is mentioned (A2).
Both surviving reports (A2, A4) reprint the same Williamsburg Herald paragraph, and no independent account or follow-up was found.
